author: hoeschec
text:
I think the answer might be found in the swap zone that forms just prior to true supply/true demand.

Drawing:

1. FTR forms and Buyers are in control. Price bounces many times. 2. Price forms a RBD as it breaks the low of FTR 1. This is also the origin of the engulf 3. Engulf of 1 4. Price RT to DP to EG on its FTB 5. Price falls and a decision is made to break the low of the engulf (# 3) 6. New low is made

The last decision made (5) is the origin of the last move that makes the swap zone confirmed. Until a new low is made at 6, price could have kept rising. Instead, the sellers were in control when price tested the first DP...that test is the FTB (4). Sellers are too strong and push price down to form a new low (6). Now any RT to the origin of the new low is the final DP before the confirmation of the swap zone. It is where the first level of fresh sell orders lies - true supply.

Price won't fakeout above the true supply until it makes a decision to make a new swap zone. A fakeout above # 5 wouldn't net the IT's any more liquidity anyway as all the OF above # 5 was accumulated/distributed in order to form the bearish controlled swap zone. The first area where fresh order flow exists would be at #5.

Is this correct?

Here is a drawing, and a real life example:

At some point, the swap zone could itself be engulfed and a new swap zone could form. I think we are safe to trade the true supply in this zone so long as one of two things are happening:

1. Price has not yet hit the target of its engulf (in this case, the target for shorts) 2. The target for shorts is itself engulfed (target hit, but low extreme of the target is engulfed, indicating price wants lower...)

In this example, as long as there is a current valid bearish engulf (meaning an engulf with a target that has not been hit) we can feel safe trading the true supply area in the bear-controlled swap zone. Once the target for shorts is hit, and no downside engulf of this target occurs, we will wait to see where the new swap zone is formed.

Once a new swap zone is confirmed, we start the same process all over again.

I could be totally wrong about this....

If you disagree, feel free to tell me.

Drawing below to illustrate:

Example where target is hit: we would wait to see what price does before trusting the true supply zone.

Example where TG for shorts is itself engulfed, Supply zone can still be trusted to hold price down.

author: hoeschec
text:
I've been reading through Marketpedia and looking at my old posts, trying to conceptualize the MPL and true supply/demand.

We know FTR's and engulfs are everywhere on a chart...there are so many of them it would be overwhelming to draw each and every FTR/FL and engulf in every time frame on the chart. We know not every engulf and FTR/FL are created equal...some are much more important than others. We focus on the most important engulfs- specifically, engulfs of established swap zones.

If True supply/demand is formed after an engulf of an important swap zone, we know the true supply/demand level is also a FTR/FL. The MPL (as Jurij helped me understand with his post last night...refer to post # 953) is always located in a FTR.

If everything I've said is true so far, then it makes sense that not all MPL's are created equal - some are much stronger than others. The term "MPL" isn't inherently special in any way...it isn't a 'magic' area where price won't break. It is simply the most extreme set of order flow left in a FL. The MPL is only as strong as the FTR/FL in which it resides. Not all FTR's are important, and not all FTR's will bounce price. Some FTR's are weaker than others. Similarly, not every MPL is going to hold price the way we might want. There is no guarantee an MPL will hold price at any given time.

When price easily engulfs FL/FTR, it was able to break the MPL included within. Easy breaking of MPL = imbalance of order flow. Example - a FTR that forms after a bearish engulf that fails to hold price down doesn't have enough sell orders to compete against the buy orders that push price back up. The stronger a FL/FTR, the stronger its MPL will be. Strong MPL's will bounce price, and we can feel comfortable trading fakeouts to these MPL's.

If we find critical areas where an engulf of a swap zone occurs, we can be relatively confident that the resulting formation of a FL/FTR (and the MPL included within the FTR) will be strong. Strong FTR = MPL that is likely to bounce price. MPL's that bounce price have a lot of order flow ready to protect its position.

As always, I could be wrong, but I want to keep track of my thoughts.

hoeschec wrote: [...] Similarly, not every MPL is going to hold price the way we might want. There is no guarantee an MPL will hold price at any given time. [...]

Hi H, I'm looking into your drawing about AU but wanted to say your last post is really golden. As you said MPL is just the extreme set of orders within a level. No one knows if it will hold or not, of course a small bounce can still happen, but not a sure thing. Why? Because only ITs decide where they want to sell. So how to know if an FL (and MPL) is likely to bounce price? RTM is all about reading ITs intention, so this is why watching approach is the real clue in all this. ITs can't hide their intentions on LTF.

This could be also an answer to your question above where you asked about MPLs that there's always an MPL above and how to know which one will hold... It is really the other way around. First comes the level, then we try to decode intentions. If there's no intention then probably it is the next level.

I have to admit this sounds easy but on real charts it is a real challenge BTW keep it up, you're asking the right questions.

author: hoeschec
text:
Would I be right in saying:

1. Every swap zone is formed when price engulfs an opposing FTR/FL that has held price down in the past, and forms a new FTR

2. The newly formed FTR is where the new fresh orders are created

3. Price 'respecting' a SR Flip is really just a swap zone forming on a lower time frame

4. Not all swap zones are created equal - some are more important than others (some have more free OF)

5. Every newly formed swap zone forms a fresh set of free OF, and this new swap zone has a target

6. Assuming we form a bullish swap zone (resistance becomes support): the target for the new swap zone is the fresh set of OF created in the FTR/FL the last time support became resistance (the origin of the move down).

7. All price does is move from decision point to decision point - from swap level to swap level.

8. Since the market is fractal, you can have LTF swap zones forming inside of a HTF swap zone
